stem: After upgrading dbt Core, a team's CI runs start printing deprecation warnings, but the pipeline still exits successfully. The team wants exactly those deprecation warnings, and only those, to fail CI, without turning every other dbt warning into a hard failure. Which flag achieves this, and why?

option_texts.A: Setting both `WARN_ERROR` and `WARN_ERROR_OPTIONS` together, to match exactly what the team wants
option_texts.B: `--warn-error`, because it converts all dbt warnings into errors, which is the safest default for CI
option_texts.C: `--fail-fast`, because it stops the run the moment a warning appears, which counts as failing CI
option_texts.D: `--warn-error-options`, because it gives granular control over exactly which types of warnings are treated as errors

drill_answer_short: --warn-error-options promotes only specific named warning types to errors
decision_hinge: The WARN_ERROR_OPTIONS config or --warn-error-options flag gives you more granular control over exactly which types of warnings are treated as errors. WARN_ERROR and WARN_ERROR_OPTIONS are mutually exclusive; you can only specify one, otherwise you'll see a usage error.

plausible_options.C: The team wants exactly those deprecation warnings, and only those, to fail CI

A.signal: The team wants exactly those deprecation warnings, and only those, to fail CI
A.requires_fact: WARN_ERROR and WARN_ERROR_OPTIONS are mutually exclusive; you can only specify one, even across different configuration sources, otherwise you'll see a usage error.

eliminated_by.B: without turning every other dbt warning into a hard failure

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — dbt rejects this combination as a usage error rather than merging the two
distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated requirement — --warn-error turns every warning into an error, not just deprecations
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — --fail-fast controls when a run stops, not which conditions count as a failure

stem: A developer runs `dbt run -s src_listings` and sees `Compilation Error in model src_listings (models/src/src_listings.sql)` followed by `'soruce' is undefined`. The team needs to identify the step in dbt's process where this kind of error is caught, and the most direct fix. What's going on?

option_texts.A: The warehouse rejected the compiled SQL because `soruce` is not a valid table name, so the error was caught by the database
option_texts.B: dbt caught an invalid Jinja reference while parsing the model; the fix is correcting the misspelled `source` call in the SQL file
option_texts.C: dbt's dependency graph contains a cycle caused by the misspelled reference
option_texts.D: The model's YAML properties file is missing a required key named `soruce`

drill_answer_short: An undefined Jinja name is a parsing-stage Compilation Error, not a database or graph error
decision_hinge: Parsing: check that the Jinja snippets in .sql files are valid, and that .yml files are valid -- Compilation Error.

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — a rejected table name at the warehouse would be a Database Error, a later step than this
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — a cycle is a Dependency Error, a different step than an undefined Jinja name
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — the error points at the SQL file's Jinja, not a missing YAML property

stem: A model named `dim_listings_cleansed` in a project named `airbnb` fails with a cryptic database error. The developer wants to open the exact SQL dbt actually sent to the warehouse for this run, not just the source `.sql` file. Where should they look?

option_texts.A: The `logs/dbt.log` file, which stores the exact SQL dbt executes for every model
option_texts.B: The `target/compiled/` directory, which contains the raw `select` statement before dbt wraps it for execution
option_texts.C: The `target/run/` directory, which contains the SQL dbt executes to build the model
option_texts.D: The original `models/` source file, since dbt executes the Jinja template directly against the warehouse

drill_answer_short: target/run contains the SQL dbt actually executes to build the model
decision_hinge: The target/compiled directory contains select statements that you can run in any query editor. The target/run directory contains the SQL dbt executes to build your models. The logs/dbt.log file contains all the queries that dbt runs, and additional logging.

plausible_options.B: wants to open the exact SQL dbt actually sent to the warehouse for this run

A.requires_fact: The target/run directory contains the SQL dbt executes to build your models; the logs/dbt.log file contains all the queries dbt runs plus additional logging, not a single authoritative file per model.

distractor_traps.A: T2: wrong layer — the log file records everything dbt runs, it is not the dedicated per-model file the error points at
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — target/compiled holds the select statement before dbt wraps it for the actual run
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt always compiles Jinja to SQL before executing anything

stem: A dbt invocation fails while dbt is checking that the project's dependency graph has no cycles, after Jinja and YAML have already parsed successfully and before any SQL is sent to the warehouse. The developer needs to name the error type dbt reports for exactly this step. Which error type is it?

option_texts.A: Runtime Error, raised while dbt initializes and connects to the warehouse
option_texts.B: Compilation Error, raised during the parsing step that checks Jinja and YAML validity, before any dependency graph is built
option_texts.C: Database Error, raised during the SQL-execution step that runs the models
option_texts.D: Dependency Error, raised during the graph-validation step that compiles dependencies into a graph and checks it's acyclic

drill_answer_short: A cycle in the dependency graph is a Dependency Error, after parsing and before SQL execution
decision_hinge: Parsing: Compilation Error. Graph validation: compile the dependencies into a graph, check that it's acyclic -- Dependency Error. SQL execution: run the models -- Database Error.

plausible_options.B: after Jinja and YAML have already parsed successfully

A.signal: checking that the project's dependency graph has no cycles
A.requires_fact: Initialize checks that this is a dbt project and that dbt can connect to the warehouse, raising a Runtime Error; graph validation is a separate, later step.

eliminated_by.C: before any SQL is sent to the warehouse

distractor_traps.A: T8: scope error — Runtime Error covers project initialization and connecting, not graph-cycle checks
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — parsing already succeeded per the stem; this failure happens one step later
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated fact — the stem says this happens before any SQL is sent

stem: A model run ends with `Database Error in model customers ... SQL compilation error: syntax error line 14 at position 4 unexpected 'from'`, and the message also names the compiled file's path. The developer needs the fastest documented way to isolate and fix this. What should they do first?

option_texts.A: Rewrite the model entirely using a different materialization, since Database Errors mean the current one is unsupported
option_texts.B: Open the compiled SQL at the path the error names, and re-execute it in a query editor to isolate the mistake
option_texts.C: Open `dbt_project.yml` and check for an unexpected top-level key instead of trying to isolate the compiled SQL, since that is the most common Database Error cause
option_texts.D: Ignore the error and rerun, since Database Errors are usually warehouse flakiness that resolves itself

drill_answer_short: 90% of the time a Database Error is a mistake in the model's SQL; re-run the compiled query to isolate it
decision_hinge: 90% of the time, there's a mistake in the SQL of your model. To fix this, open the compiled SQL and try to re-execute it to isolate the error, for example by copying the compiled query into a query runner and executing it.

plausible_options.C: The developer needs the fastest documented way to isolate and fix this

eliminated_by.A: SQL compilation error: syntax error line 14 at position 4 unexpected 'from'
eliminated_by.D: the message also names the compiled file's path

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — a syntax mistake is not evidence the materialization itself is unsupported
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — an unexpected dbt_project.yml key causes a different error, not a Database Error
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — the documented guidance is that most Database Errors trace to a real SQL mistake

stem: An incremental model configured with `on_schema_change='fail'` starts erroring after a new column appears upstream. The developer needs two genuinely useful next steps before deciding how to fix it, not a guess. Which TWO are useful debugging steps?

option_texts.A: Confirm exactly which columns differ between the source query and the existing target table
option_texts.B: Decide whether the new column should be added going forward with `append_new_columns`, or handled with a full rebuild
option_texts.C: Switch `on_schema_change` to `ignore` immediately, since that always resolves schema-change errors safely
option_texts.D: Delete the model's YAML column definitions, since schema changes are always a YAML configuration problem

drill_answer_short: Confirm the actual column diff, then choose append_new_columns or a full rebuild
decision_hinge: The possible values for on_schema_change are: ignore, the default behavior; fail, triggers an error message when the source and target schemas diverge; append_new_columns, append new columns to the existing table. None of the on_schema_change behaviors backfill values in old records for newly added columns.

plausible_options.C: The developer needs two genuinely useful next steps before deciding how to fix it, not a guess

eliminated_by.D: starts erroring after a new column appears upstream

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — ignore is a real setting, but switching to it blindly does not confirm what actually changed
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — a new upstream column is a data and config decision, not a missing YAML key

stem: A developer runs `dbt run -s dim_listings` and gets `Relation "dev_zoltan"."src_listings" does not exist`. The schema name `dev_zoltan` matches their own configured target schema. The team needs the two most likely explanations for a missing relation like this. Which TWO are plausible causes?

option_texts.A: The upstream model or source that builds `src_listings` has not been run yet in this environment
option_texts.B: The developer previewed the query or selected only a downstream model without first running its upstream parents
option_texts.C: dbt always builds every model into exactly one global schema shared by all developers, so the relation should already exist
option_texts.D: The `generate_schema_name` macro silently drops a developer's `src_listings` relations older than 30 days

drill_answer_short: The upstream relation simply has not been built yet in this developer's own schema
decision_hinge: You'll need to make sure you have executed dbt run for any upstream models, otherwise dbt will try to select from tables and views that haven't been built. Each dbt user has their own target schema for development.

plausible_options.C: The schema name `dev_zoltan` matches their own configured target schema

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — each developer has their own target schema, so nothing guarantees the relation already exists there
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt has no such automatic relation-expiry behaviour

stem: A macro file fails to compile with `Reached EOF without finding a close tag for macro (searched from line 1)`. The developer needs to know what kind of mistake typically causes this exact message, besides a missing `{% endmacro %}`. What else commonly triggers it?

option_texts.A: A `not_null` test failing on a column referenced inside the macro
option_texts.B: A missing semicolon at the end of the model's final `select` statement
option_texts.C: Forgetting a closing `}` in a Jinja tag, or closing a `for` loop before closing an enclosing `if` statement
option_texts.D: The warehouse connection timing out while dbt waits for the macro to run

drill_answer_short: Mismatched Jinja tags, like closing a for loop before an enclosing if, also trigger this EOF error
decision_hinge: This particular example is for a forgotten {% endmacro %} tag, but you can also get errors like this for forgetting a closing }, or closing a for loop before closing an if statement.

eliminated_by.A: A macro file fails to compile with `Reached EOF without finding a close tag for macro (searched from line 1)`
eliminated_by.D: fails to compile with `Reached EOF without finding a close tag for macro (searched from line 1)`

distractor_traps.A: T2: wrong layer — a failing test runs after a successful build; it cannot cause a compile-time EOF error
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a SQL punctuation mistake is a different failure mode than an unclosed Jinja tag
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — this error happens at parse time, before any connection is needed

stem: A model build fails with a Database Error citing a SQL syntax mistake. The developer needs two genuinely useful documented ways to isolate exactly where the SQL is wrong. Which TWO are useful approaches?

option_texts.A: Open the compiled SQL file in the `target/` directory and re-execute it directly in a query editor
option_texts.B: Use the `Preview` button, equivalent to grabbing the compiled select statement and running it to see the results
option_texts.C: Edit the file inside `target/` directly and rerun `dbt run`, since that is the fastest way to apply a fix
option_texts.D: Delete the `logs/` directory so dbt regenerates a cleaner compiled SQL file

drill_answer_short: Open the compiled SQL in target/ or use Preview, both of which run the compiled select statement
decision_hinge: While debugging a model or data test, it's often useful to execute the underlying select statement to find the source of the bug. You can find these compiled SQL files in the target/ directory. The Preview button executes whatever SQL statement is in the active tab, equivalent to grabbing the compiled select statement from the target/compiled directory and running it.

plausible_options.C: The developer needs two genuinely useful documented ways to isolate exactly where the SQL is wrong

eliminated_by.D: A model build fails with a Database Error citing a SQL syntax mistake

distractor_traps.C: T7: over-engineering — editing a generated file is explicitly discouraged; a real fix belongs in the source model
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — deleting logs does not change or regenerate compiled SQL

stem: A file `tests/dim_listings_minimum_nights.sql` contains `SELECT * FROM {{ model }} WHERE minimum_nights < 1`, placed directly in the `tests/` directory as a singular test. Running `dbt test` fails with `Compilation Error: 'model' is undefined`. The developer needs the actual cause. What's wrong?

option_texts.A: Every singular test file must directly include a `{% test %}` block, which this file is missing
option_texts.B: The `tests/` directory only accepts `.yml` files, so `.sql` files placed there are never parsed
option_texts.C: `dbt test` must be run with a `--select` flag naming which model `{{ model }}` refers to
option_texts.D: Singular tests don't receive a `model` variable; only a generic test's `test` block receives `model` as a parameter, so this file should use `ref()` or `source()` directly

drill_answer_short: Only a generic test block receives model as a parameter; singular tests reference models with ref() directly
decision_hinge: A generic data test is defined in a test block, which contains a parameterized query and accepts arguments such as model and column_name. A singular data test is the exact SQL that will return failing records, using ref and source just like a model, and is placed in the tests directory.

plausible_options.A: placed directly in the `tests/` directory as a singular test

eliminated_by.B: contains `SELECT * FROM {{ model }} WHERE minimum_nights < 1`, placed directly in the `tests/` directory
eliminated_by.C: Running `dbt test` fails with `Compilation Error: 'model' is undefined`

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — a test block defines a generic test; a singular test needs no test block at all
distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — the tests/ directory is exactly where singular SQL tests belong
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — no flag supplies a `model` variable to a singular test

stem: A macro calls `{{ log("Call your mom!") }}` and then `{{ log("Call your dad!", info=True) }}`. A developer runs `dbt run` and watches the terminal output directly, without opening any log file. The team needs to know exactly which message(s) appear on screen. What do they see?

option_texts.A: Both messages, because `log()` always writes to stdout regardless of the `info` argument
option_texts.B: Only "Call your dad!", because `info=True` is required for a message to also print to stdout
option_texts.C: Neither message, because `log()` only ever writes to the log file, never to the terminal
option_texts.D: Only "Call your mom!", because the first `log()` call in a macro always takes priority

drill_answer_short: log() writes to stdout only when info=True; otherwise it only writes to the log file
decision_hinge: log() takes an info argument: if False, write to the log file; if True, write to both the log file and stdout. The default is False.

plausible_options.A: watches the terminal output directly, without opening any log file

eliminated_by.D: runs `dbt run` and watches the terminal output directly

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — the default behaviour writes only to the log file, not the terminal
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated fact — the second call explicitly sets info=True, which does reach stdout
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — log() has no such call-order priority rule
